{{short description|British-American physicist}}
'''Edgar Lipworth''' (1923 – 14 July 1977) was an American physicist,<ref name=Chretien>{{cite journal|author=Chretien, Max|title=Obituary. Edgar Lipworth|journal=Physics Today|volume=31|issue=1|pages=93–94|doi=10.1063/1.3001845|doi-access=free}}</ref> specializing "in research in molecular and atomic beams, nuclear physics, lasers and the symmetry of physical laws under time reversal."<ref name=NYT>{{cite news|title=Edgar Lipworth, 53, a Physicist, Is Dead|newspaper=NY Times|date=15 July 1977|page=23|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/07/15/archives/edgar-lipworth-53-a-physicist-is-dead-brandeis-professor-is.html}}</ref>

Born and educated in England, Edgar Lipworth worked from 1944 to 1946 as a civilian research assistant on radar for the [[Air Ministry]]. After graduating with a BA from the [[University of Manchester]] in 1947, he became a graduate student in physics at [[Manhattan]]'s [[Columbia University]]. There he obtained his PhD with advisor [[Willis Lamb]] with a dissertation on measurement of the [[Lamb shift]] in singly ionized helium.<ref name=Chretien/> From 1953 to 1954 Lipworth held a fellowship with [[Radio Corporation of America|RCA]]. He also was a consultant at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] and received research grants from the [[National Science Foundation]].<ref name=NYT/>

{{blockquote|From 1956 to 1961 he held a position at the Radiation Laboratory in Berkeley, working there on spins and magnetic properties of radioactive nuclei using the Rabi beam method. Lipworth joined the Brandeis physics department in the fall of 1961, a time when its graduate program was only five years old and entirely oriented towards theoretical physics. Together with [[Stephan Berko]] he succeeded in building up an impressive experimental research program in a very short time. A magnetic resonance apparatus with a high electric field allowed him to study the [[Stark shift]]s in the Zeeman and hyperfine structure of atoms.<ref name=Chretien/>}}

Lipworth was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] and served as the chair of its Division of Electron and Atomic Physics in 1966–1967. He spent the academic year 1974–1975 at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]] as a [[Guggenheim Fellow]].<ref name=Chretien/>

He married Anna Rashbaum when he was a graduate student at Columbia University. He died at age 53 in [[Cape Town]], when he was on a leave of absence for the academic year 1976–1977. He was survived by his widow, a son, and a daughter.<ref name=NYT/>
